property_summary: For any caller and _accessControl, calling initialize(...) on the correct contract always makes the contract report that it is initialized as an implementation for UUPS (proxiableUUID() callable in non-delegated context), whereas the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() leaves the UUPS-initialized invariant unset and thus causes proxiableUUID() to revert when called in the non-delegated context for some inputs (caller context); the test fuzzes caller address to find a context where mutant differs.

For any caller address used to call initialize, calling proxiableUUID() on the contract in a non-delegated context must return the ERC1967 IMPLEMENTATION_SLOT (i.e. succeed) after initialize(...) on the reference C, whereas the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() can leave the contract in a context where proxiableUUID() reverts for some caller addresses — so the property is that initialize(...) always makes proxiableUUID() callable (non-reverting) from the external EOA caller that invoked initialize.

For every caller address that invokes initialize(accessControl), the reference C leaves the implementation contract in a non-delegated callable UUPS state so that calling proxiableUUID() (non-delegated call) succeeds; the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() can leave proxiableUUID() reverting for some callers, so there exists a caller address input that makes proxiableUUID() revert after initialize on the mutant but not on the reference.

For every caller address and accessControl value, calling initialize(...) on the correct contract sets the UUPS initializable state so that immediately afterwards calling proxiableUUID() externally (non-delegated) returns the ERC1967 implementation slot (does not revert); the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() can leave the contract so proxiableUUID() reverts for some caller addresses — our test fuzzes the caller address to find such a counterexample.

For every caller address, after calling initialize(accessControl) the reference contract always allows an external non-delegated call to proxiableUUID() (it does not revert and returns the ERC1967 slot), whereas the mutant that omits __UUPSUpgradeable_init() can leave proxiableUUID() reverting for some caller addresses (so there exists a caller input making proxiableUUID() revert on the mutant but not on the reference).

For any caller and any _accessControl address, calling initialize(...) on the correct contract sets the internal initialized flag so that a second initialize call reverts (cannot re-initialize); the mutant that omits setting _initialized allows re-initialization (so a second initialize call succeeds) for some inputs.

After any successful top-level initialize(...) call, the reference contract permanently marks itself initialized so that a subsequent call to initialize(...) from the same caller (or any caller) reverts; the mutant that does not set _initialized allows a second initialize call to succeed for some inputs, so the property is that a second initialize attempt MUST revert (reference) and the mutant will sometimes not revert.

For any caller and any accessControl address, calling initialize(...) twice: the reference always reverts (cannot re-initialize a contract marked initialized after the first top-level initialize), whereas the mutant that fails to set the initialized flag may allow the second initialize to succeed for some inputs.

For any caller and any _accessControl address, calling initialize(...) via a DELEGATECALL context (i.e. through a proxy where address(this).code.length == 0) must succeed on the reference (it treats construction case specially) but the mutant that never sets _initialized breaks the construction-path invariant causing the initializer modifier to accept construction but fail later expectations; specifically, after a top-level initialize called from a deployed proxy (address with empty code) the reference marks initializing state transitions correctly so that a subsequent check of proxiableUUID() via notDelegated/onlyProxy contexts behaves consistently — the mutant allows inconsistent initialization state for proxy contexts and can cause the notDelegated check to revert when calling proxiableUUID(), so the property asserts that a call to proxiableUUID() on the implementation (not delegated) always returns the ERC1967 slot after initialize is called on the proxied instance (reference: returns slot, mutant: may revert), and the test fuzzes the _accessControl address to find a failing input.

For any accessControl address, a top-level call to initialize(address) on the implementation contract (called directly) always completes (does not revert) and sets the contract into initializing/completed state so that immediately after the call the contract's proxiableUUID() can be called via notDelegated (i.e. calling proxiableUUID() on the implementation directly) and returns the ERC1967 implementation slot; the mutant that omits setting _initialized may leave initialization markers inconsistent and cause proxiableUUID() (which is guarded by notDelegated) to revert for some inputs.

For any vault/asset and storage state, calling rate updates utilizationData.lastUpdate to block.timestamp and returns a value computed using elapsed = block.timestamp - previous lastUpdate when block.timestamp > previous lastUpdate; the mutant that forces elapsed=0 breaks this because it will return a different rate for cases where block.timestamp > previous lastUpdate and previous lastUpdate != block.timestamp.

For any vault/asset pair and stored utilizationData where utilizationData.lastUpdate < block.timestamp and utilizationData.index != currentUtilizationIndex, calling rate updates lastUpdate to block.timestamp and returns a value computed using elapsed = block.timestamp - previous lastUpdate (i.e., the call succeeds and elapsed>0 is used); the mutant forcing elapsed=0 will still succeed but will produce a different returned rate for some fuzzed inputs, so the reference's returned value must equal the value computed when using elapsed = block.timestamp - previous lastUpdate.

For any vault, asset and prior stored utilization state where utilizationData.lastUpdate < block.timestamp and currentUtilizationIndex != utilizationData.index, calling rate(...) updates lastUpdate to block.timestamp and returns the same value as calling the reference computation that uses elapsed = block.timestamp - previous lastUpdate; the mutant that forces elapsed=0 will for some fuzzed (vault,asset,previous index,lastUpdate,block.timestamp) produce a different returned latestAnswer, so the property (returned value equals the value computed using true elapsed) holds for the reference but is violated by the mutant.

For any vault/asset and prior stored utilization state where utilizationData.lastUpdate < block.timestamp and utilizationData.index != currentIndex, calling rate(...) completes successfully and updates utilizationData.lastUpdate to block.timestamp and returns a value computed using elapsed = block.timestamp - previous lastUpdate; the mutant that forces elapsed=0 preserves success and lastUpdate update but can produce a different returned latestAnswer for some fuzzed inputs, so the reference's returned value equals the computed-with-true-elapsed value while the mutant can differ.

For any vault/asset and current stored utilizationData where utilizationData.lastUpdate < block.timestamp and currentUtilizationIndex != utilizationData.index, calling rate(_) returns the same latestAnswer as computing elapsed = block.timestamp - previous lastUpdate and passing that elapsed into _applySlopes; the mutant that forces elapsed=0 violates this (for some fuzzed inputs the returned latestAnswer differs).

For any call to rate(vault,asset), the reference contract returns a value computed from the current utilization (when block.timestamp <= lastUpdate it uses IVault.utilization) — the mutant instead treats that case as zero, so there exist inputs where returned rate differs (i.e., reference's rate equals _applySlopes(..., IVault.utilization(...), ...) for all inputs, but mutant can return _applySlopes(..., 0, ...) for some inputs).

For any vault and asset and storage state, C.rate(...) always uses IVault(_vault).utilization(_asset) when block.timestamp <= utilizationData.lastUpdate; the mutant instead uses zero in that case, so there exist inputs (vault,asset and lastUpdate >= block.timestamp) where the returned rate differs.

For any vault, asset, and current chain time, if the stored utilizationData.lastUpdate is >= block.timestamp then C.rate(...) always queries IVault.utilization(_asset) (the reference returns the rate computed from that on-chain utilization), whereas the mutant returns a rate computed as if utilization were zero — so the reference's returned rate equals _applySlopes(..., IVault.utilization(...), ...) for all admissible inputs, but the mutant can differ when lastUpdate >= block.timestamp and IVault.utilization(...) != 0.

For any vault and asset and current chain time, if the stored utilizationData.lastUpdate is >= block.timestamp then C.rate(...) reads IVault.utilization(_asset) to compute the returned rate; the mutant instead uses zero in that case, so there exist inputs (vault, asset, and stored lastUpdate) where the returned rate differs.

For any vault and asset and chain time, when C.rate is called and utilizationData.lastUpdate >= block.timestamp the reference contract always queries IVault(_vault).utilization(_asset) to compute and return the rate, whereas the mutant returns the rate computed with utilization == 0 in that case, so there exist (vault,asset,lastUpdate,utilization) inputs where returned values differ.

For all inputs, the reference C rejects any SlopeData with kink == 0 (reverting InvalidKink) while the mutant incorrectly accepts kink == 0; therefore the property: calling setSlopes with a slope whose kink is zero must always revert on the reference but may succeed on the mutant.

For all inputs, the reference C reverts when setSlopes is called with a SlopeData whose kink == 0 (InvalidKink), whereas the mutant accepts kink == 0 and thus call succeeds for some inputs — so the property is that setSlopes MUST revert whenever _slopes.kink == 0.

For all inputs the reference contract always reverts when setSlopes is called with SlopeData.kink == 0, but the mutant accepts kink == 0 (does not revert) for some inputs; the test fuzzes slope fields and asserts that calling setSlopes with kink == 0 always reverts (ok == false) on the reference.

For every input where kink >= 1e27 the call to setSlopes must revert (InvalidKink); the mutant only reverts for kink >= 1e27 but (incorrectly) would accept kink == 0 — however we instead assert a different universal rule: for any slopes.kink that is either 0 or >=1e27, the reference always reverts iff kink == 0 or kink >= 1e27 (i.e. reference rejects kink==0 and kink>=1e27) while the mutant accepts kink==0, so fuzzing will find a kink==0 where the reference reverts but the mutant does not.

For all inputs, the reference contract always reverts when setSlopes is called with SlopeData.kink == 0, whereas the mutant accepts kink == 0 (does not revert) for some inputs — so the property: calling setSlopes with kink == 0 must always revert.

For any SlopeData input, the reference contract reverts when kink is 0 or >= 1e27 (i.e. setSlopes only accepts 0<kink<1e27); the mutant removes that validation so there exist inputs (kink == 0 or kink >= 1e27) that the mutant accepts but the reference rejects.

For any SlopeData passed to setSlopes, the reference C reverts (refuses) when slopes.kink == 0 or slopes.kink >= 1e27, while the mutant accepts such kink values; the test fuzzes kink and asserts whether setSlopes call succeeded (reference always reverts for those edge kinks, mutant will sometimes succeed).

For all inputs, the reference C reverts when given a SlopeData.kink equal to 0 or >= 1e27, while the mutant accepts at least some of those kink values (i.e. there exist kink values where reference reverts but mutant call succeeds).

For every SlopeData passed to setSlopes, the reference contract either accepts it only when 0 < kink < 1e27, and in particular if kink == 0 then the reference always reverts while the mutant (which removed the check) may accept it — the property asserted is: for any fuzzed kink, calling setSlopes with kink == 0 must revert on the reference (so the call does not succeed); the mutant that removed validation will allow success for some inputs.

For every SlopeData input the reference C reverts when called with kink == 1e27 (the reference treats kink >= 1e27 as invalid), so calling setSlopes with kink == 1e27 always fails on the reference but the mutant (which removed validation) will accept that exact kink value; the test fuzzes slope0 and slope1 while fixing kink to 1e27 to distinguish them.

For any input kink the reference contract accepts only slopes where kink != 0 and kink < 1e27 (i.e., setSlopes succeeds iff kink is nonzero and less than 1e27); the mutant inverts the check allowing kink == 0 and thus will accept at least one input (kink == 0) that the reference rejects.

For every input slopes.kink the reference C rejects kink == 0 (reverts) and accepts 0 < kink < 1e27 (succeeds); the mutant instead accepts kink == 0, so there exists an input (kink == 0) where the mutant's setSlopes returns success but the reference reverts.

For all SlopeData inputs, the reference C rejects (reverts) when slopes.kink == 0 and accepts (succeeds) for 0 < slopes.kink < 1e27; the mutant inverts this allowing kink == 0 (so there exists an input kink==0 where mutant succeeds but reference reverts).

For all inputs, the reference contract rejects (reverts) when slopes.kink == 0 and accepts (succeeds) when 0 < slopes.kink < 1e27; the mutant instead accepts kink == 0, so there exists an input with kink==0 where the mutant succeeds but the reference reverts.

For every SlopeData input, the reference C accepts (setSlopes succeeds) iff kink is non-zero and less than 1e27; the mutant accepts kink == 0 (making it accept at least one input—kink == 0—that the reference rejects), so there exists a fuzz input where reference reverts but mutant succeeds.
